paras: The peonage of Will Waters was the seizure, whipping and forced return to work of Waters, a Black farm laborer, by three young white farmers of Jasper County, Georgia, in 1903, after he left his employer while in debt. William Shy, Arthur Glawson and Robert Turner pleaded guilty in the federal court at Macon on June 24, 1903, and Judge Emory Speer fined each $1,000 but suspended most of the fine. Speer called it the first such crime he knew of in Georgia, and papers often printed the case beside the Alabama peonage conviction of J. W. Pace.

According to the account given at the Macon hearing, Waters had contracted to work for Shy from January to August, fell about $35 in debt to him, and left to work for Pounds & Roberts in Jones County. At sentencing, Speer described him as a "person of color who had obtained an advance upon his contract" and quit in a way that caused one defendant a loss.

Shy, accompanied by Turner, followed Waters and brought him back to Jasper County, using a buggy whip on his back. Later features in the National Tribune and the Louisville Courier-Journal said the two men tied him to the back axle of their buggy and whipped him on the way, the Courier-Journal adding that he was dragged part of the way. Shy then held Waters at work until Waters's wife went to Macon and reported the case.

On June 18, in his charge to the federal grand jury at Macon, Speer described an unnamed case in which an employer and others armed themselves, seized a worker at his new job, tied and whipped him, and forced him back to work. That night federal deputies brought Shy, Glawson and Turner to Macon together with Waters, and the three were bound over to the grand jury on $1,000 bond each. The warrant charged them with "forcibly deporting" Waters from Jones County to Jasper County, "whipping and otherwise misusing him."

On the morning of June 24 the three pleaded guilty before Speer in a crowded courtroom. Speer noted a maximum penalty of five years or a $5,000 fine, granted that they had "no conception" they were breaking federal law, and warned that the problems of "this people" would be "fearfully intensified" by any attempt to solve them "by the bullet or the lash." He fined each $1,000 but suspended the sentence during good behavior once each had paid $100 and one-third of the costs of prosecution. In July the chairman of the Georgia Prison Commission called it the only peonage case before the state's courts in several years.

Georgia papers gave the case prominent space: the Savannah Morning News put Speer's charge on its front page under "PEONAGE IN GEORGIA," and the Atlanta Constitution printed his sentencing remarks in full. A brief June 24 wire, which called the defendants "prominent farmers" who "caught a negro" in debt to them, ran from Birmingham and Montgomery to South Carolina and Ohio. The Minneapolis Journal called involuntary servitude "a most serious crime," and the National Tribune wrote that "there is nobody to take the poor negro's part." The Courier-Journal's correspondent blamed a "poor white trash element" but described Waters's flight as "the usual negro custom."

Black newspapers carried the case as reprinted wire and Macon items, without editorial comment. The Cleveland Gazette printed Speer's charge under "HELD IN SAVERY" [Slavery] and later reported the fines for holding "an Afro-American in involuntary servitude," while the St. Louis Palladium headed the wire "NEGRO HELD IN SERVITUDE." The American Baptist wrote that three young white men had held "a colored man in practical slavery contrary to law," and the Savannah Tribune was the only Black paper found to name Waters.

The June 18 Macon dispatch named the victim "William Walters" and later accounts Waters, and the defendants' names appeared as Sly, Shey, Clawson and Glosson, with Turner as both Robert and Frank. The Iowa Bystander gave the fine as $1,500 against the $1,000 of Speer's recorded sentence, and the Dawson News put the plea on a Saturday rather than Wednesday, June 24.

bases: Three farmers seized a laborer who had left his contract in debt, whipped him and forced him back to work, and pleaded guilty to holding him in involuntary servitude (A4, A16, A6).
Separate Macon reports of the warrant hearing (A1, A4) and of the guilty pleas and sentence (A16, A6) agree on the defendants, the victim and the charge, and the defendants confessed in court (A16).

accounts.gist: An employee who left for another employer was seized at work by his former employer and others, who armed themselves, tied him, carried him back, whipped him and forced him to work; he was 'now being held practically in servitude'.

accounts.label: Warrant (June 18 dispatch)
accounts.gist: The three were charged with forcibly deporting Waters from a Jones County plantation to Jasper County and whipping and otherwise misusing him.

accounts.label: Speer's sentencing remarks
accounts.gist: The defendants held a citizen in involuntary servitude by force and violence after he took an advance and quit; Speer allowed that they did not know they were breaking federal law and suspended most of the fine.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: The young men, 'prominent farmers', caught a negro in debt to them, whipped him and made him work for them; fined $1,000 each, suspended on $100 each.

accounts.label: Magazine-style features (National Tribune, Courier-Journal)
accounts.gist: Waters drew advances, was told he owed $35 beyond his contract, left at night, was traced, tied to a buggy axle and whipped on the way back (the Courier-Journal adds dragged part of the way); his wife swore out warrants.

framing.detail: Georgia papers reported the case at length as a federal prosecution: Savannah Morning News front-page 'PEONAGE IN GEORGIA'; Atlanta Constitution 'PLEAD GUILTY TO CHARGE' with Speer's full remarks.
The June 24 wire called the defendants 'prominent farmers' and was often set beside the Pace conviction in Alabama.
Minneapolis Journal: holding a man in involuntary servitude 'a most serious crime'; National Tribune: 'nobody to take the poor negro's part'.
Courier-Journal correspondent condemned a 'poor white trash element' and peonage built on 'fraud, violence and misrepresentation' but wrote of Waters's flight as 'the usual negro custom'.
Dawson News headline 'Peonage Offenders Punished' with subhead 'Judge Speer Passed Sentence On Negro Holders'.
Black papers ran the wire and Macon dispatches with headlines such as 'HELD IN SAVERY', 'NEGRO HELD IN SERVITUDE' and 'PEONAGE CASE DISPOSED OF', without editorial comment.
The American Baptist noted the men had held 'a colored man in practical slavery contrary to law'; the Cleveland Gazette used 'Afro-American'.

conflicts.note: The later local Macon reports and the hearing account use Waters.
Speer's own words in the Atlanta Constitution give $1,000; the Iowa Bystander figure is an outlier in an otherwise identical wire text.
